implementation_notes: Modern C++ has no container in the standard library, but the classic locator collapses into a type-keyed map: std::type_index from typeid as the key, std::any as the type-erased slot, any_cast<T> for checked retrieval, and template set<T>()/get<T>() so call sites stay typed. Where the services are polymorphic, register std::shared_ptr<Iface> or a std::function factory instead of a value in std::any, so callers depend on the interface. Prefer passing the registry (or an explicit AppContext of typed fields) down from main; a function-local static locator is the global fallback, and it orders correctly because it is constructed on first use.
pitfalls: std::any requires a copy-constructible payload, so move-only services cannot be stored; hold std::shared_ptr<Iface> or a std::function factory slot instead.
get() throws std::out_of_range for an unknown key and std::bad_any_cast for a mismatched type: on non-exceptional paths use find() with any_cast<T>(&slot) and handle nullptr.
A registry in a namespace-scope object is exposed to the static-initialisation order fiasco - construct it on first use (function-local static) or start it from main.

variants.name: Name-keyed factory registry (C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: The JNDI-shaped realization, and the one that works before C++17: keys are strings taken from configuration (file, environment, command line) and the values are factories returning a std::shared_ptr to the service interface, so the registry can create singletons or fresh instances per lookup. std::function keeps the registration side simple (a lambda per implementation) and shared_ptr settles ownership, while the interface pointer keeps callers independent of the concrete class. Choose this when names must come from deployment configuration; choose the type-keyed form when the caller knows the service type statically.
pitfalls: String keys are unchecked: a typo or a renamed binding throws only when that deployment path runs, so validate configured names once at startup.
A factory that captures a reference to a temporary or a local service outlives its capture - register factories that own or share their dependencies.
Returning raw pointers or references from the registry re-introduces the lifetime question the factory was supposed to answer; keep shared_ptr or document the ownership transfer.
